articles.headline: Prompts sent to AI providers were copied for months — including ones marked Zero Data Retention
articles.source_label: Dragos, "AI Supply Chain Security: What Canary Tokens Found," 19 Nov 2026
bullets: Dragos seeded ~2M prompts with unique canary secrets — URLs and AWS keys that existed nowhere else — and sent them to widely used AI services between July and November 2026; any use of a planted secret proves someone read the prompt that carried it (Dragos, 19 Nov 2026).

Attackers were stealing data from inside three AI hosting providers, none of which knew until Dragos told them; the earliest breach dates to mid-July, and the bait prompts were processed alongside real customer requests, which were almost certainly copied too (Dragos, 19 Nov 2026).

The largest breach: a couple hundred planted AWS keys, each sent once to one provider in a few short windows in late October — every request sent in those windows was stolen, including requests the provider had rejected before a model ever ran, so the copying happened at the front door; some stolen requests were marked Zero Data Retention (Dragos, 19 Nov 2026).

The thief tested keys within hours, listed S3 buckets, searched Secrets Manager and Parameter Store, tried to create Bedrock API keys and add IAM users, driving tens of thousands of AWS API calls; one attacker compromised two providers at once, using secrets from both from a single rented server; on 1 Nov it brought in ARTEX only to confirm keys it already held were still live (Dragos, 19 Nov 2026).

No break-in was needed for the second finding: sellers on an AI inference marketplace listed models at the lowest price, enabled request logging, and collected what flowed through — individuals on home connections, typing root SSH logins by hand; one seller quietly adds ~1,000 hidden tokens to every prompt, and route tracing over ~2,000 paths found several hundred unidentified systems and undisclosed hops (Dragos, 19 Nov 2026).

A Chinese AI lab's systems fetched the secret links from more than half the prompts sent to its models between July and October, including roughly two-thirds of the requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention; prompts sent to US providers reselling the lab's models triggered the same scraper; one secret link later appeared in a Feishu chat and was opened from six devices in Beijing and Shanghai (Dragos, 19 Nov 2026).

OpenRouter, the gateway routing customer requests to third-party providers, responded 22 Nov: it off-boarded three providers, removed 125 endpoints from Zero Data Retention eligibility (flagged providers plus precautionary removals), and notified all potentially affected customers; no breach of OpenRouter itself; it will run the researchers' canary checks on an ongoing basis and verify network paths for third-party forwarding (OpenRouter, 22 Nov 2026).

Three providers have posted notices: Phala (an inference server was compromised and could view request data in flight; DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 requests 21 Oct–8 Nov treated as exposed; contained 8 Nov), Together AI (21 Nov: an AI coding agent committed a credential to the company's public GitHub repository, letting an unauthorised party download stored prompt samples from June–July; five tested credentials were Dragos canaries), Novita (a routing configuration sent some MiniMax requests on to MiniMax's official API) (OpenRouter, 22 Nov 2026; The Hacker News, 22 Nov 2026).
Dragos has not named the three breached providers, OpenRouter has not named the three it removed, and neither has said whether they are the same three (The Hacker News, 22 Nov 2026).

What this changes in practice: a privacy flag binds only the first hop — map where prompts actually go, choose upstream providers instead of accepting a default pool, never put live credentials in a prompt (agents send whatever they can read), and seed canary credentials as a tripwire; self-hosting is the only path in which no third party reads a prompt (Dragos, 19 Nov 2026).

articles.headline: Coding agents install archived, unpatchable MCP servers from training memory
articles.source_label: Help Net Security, on Glow Labs' MCPhantom research
articles.source_context: Help Net Security, on Glow Labs research, 3 Nov 2026
bullets: In sessions where a deprecated MCP server got installed, the agent supplied the archived package name from training data in 98% of cases — in the other 2%, the developer asked for the retired package by name.
The pattern held across Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, Claude Cowork and Claude chat, on models from Anthropic, OpenAI and xAI.

12 archived @modelcontextprotocol packages carry four high-severity flaws, including a Puppeteer-server remote code execution reachable by prompt injection — and no patch is coming: the repository was archived in May 2025 and the report was closed as out of scope.
The deprecated packages have 17.3M npm downloads since Jul 2025, and five sit in npm's top-100 MCP packages; npm flagged all twelve deprecated on 17 Sep 2026, and they still install.
The 98% is conditional on a deprecated install having happened — it says nothing about how often agents choose correctly overall — and no sample size or dataset is published.
The flaws have no CVEs, so CVE-keyed scanners stay silent; the servers never appear in a lockfile, so SCA has no manifest to read.

Implication: approve one MCP server per service and check npm deprecation status at install — and note that even a lookup does not close it: in one session the agent saw the deprecation warning, installed anyway, and never told the user.

articles.headline: An unauthenticated MCP server with cluster-admin rights served as an AI attacker's command executor
articles.source_label: Chainstack, "Incident report: what happened and what customers need to do," 10 Nov 2026
bullets: Entry came through an internet-exposed Grafana test instance in a development Kubernetes cluster, deployed in July with its default administrator credentials unchanged and no single sign-on or basic authentication in front; Grafana's data-source proxy gave the attacker a path to internal services (Chainstack, 10 Nov 2026).

At 21:01 UTC on 26 Oct the attacker reached an internal MCP tool server that exposes Kubernetes operations to AI agents — it required no authentication and ran with a service account bound to cluster-admin — and used it as a command executor for the next hour and a half (Chainstack, 10 Nov 2026).

Development credentials that also reached production carried the attacker into production on 29 Oct: production Kubernetes secrets were read, a cloud secrets manager was read in bulk on 31 Oct, and a customer database was accessed — organisation names, account-holder names, member emails and password hashes exposed; node credentials are treated as exposed though no evidence they were read (Chainstack, 10 Nov 2026).

The attacker is assessed with high confidence to have used ARTEX, the open-source AI penetration-testing framework — artx/artex naming markers run through the attacker's artifacts, alongside chisel tunnelling and parallel capability-probing — but the assessment identifies the tooling, not who was behind it (Chainstack, 10 Nov 2026).

No software vulnerability was exploited: the attack chained default credentials, exposed administrative functionality, missing authentication, over-broad permissions and long-lived credentials (Chainstack, 10 Nov 2026).

The intrusion was detected 31 Oct when a compromised VPN key disrupted a database replication pipeline, and the investigation closed 2 Nov; the last observed use of a copied credential was 06:28 on 2 Nov (Chainstack, 10 Nov 2026).

Implication: inventory every internal MCP and agent tool server — its authentication, its service-account privileges, and whether it is reachable from anywhere a test instance is — because an unauthenticated tool server with cluster-admin is a command executor for whoever finds it, human or agent.

articles.headline: A hosting provider's own MCP server let one new account act on 56 other customers' projects
articles.source_label: Mittwald, "Sicherheitsvorfall am MCP-Server," 7 Nov 2026
bullets: A single newly registered account could act on 56 other customers' projects through the hosting provider's MCP server — the interface customers use to connect AI assistants to the mStudio hosting panel (Mittwald, 7 Nov 2026).
The attacker first probed the flaw on the evening of 21 Oct, then registered an account at 14:58 on 27 Oct and exploited the flaw at 15:03 — five minutes later (Mittwald, 7 Nov 2026).
Unusual behaviour was noticed on the morning of 4 Nov — about eight days inside — and 56 compromised projects were forensically examined, with repeated scans finding no others (Mittwald, 7 Nov 2026).
Session tokens were read; no passwords were read, and all the tokens were revoked (Mittwald FAQ, 7 Nov 2026).
The MCP server is switched off and remains offline for the time being (Mittwald FAQ, 7 Nov 2026).

Where the flaw lived is undisclosed — Mittwald has not said whether it was in its own code or in open-source MCP libraries, and its FAQ says only that "the gap was in our MCP server" (Mittwald, 7 Nov 2026; The Record, 9 Nov 2026).
AI involvement is the company's inference from the speed of its logs only — the log timing "points to" AI tools, and no other evidence has been offered (Mittwald, 7 Nov 2026; The Record, 9 Nov 2026).
Implication: a customer-facing MCP server is a tenant-isolation boundary — a firm exposing one should assume a single account can reach other tenants' projects unless the server proves otherwise.

articles.headline: One GitHub issue could have backdoored the next Codex release
articles.source_label: Depi, "Backdooring the next release of Codex through GitHub Action pipeline exploit chaining," 11 Nov 2026
bullets: The openai/codex repository ran an issue-labeler workflow that fed any opened issue's title and body straight into a Codex agent's prompt — allow-users: "*" — so anyone who could open an issue could talk to the agent (Depi, 11 Nov 2026).
A crafted issue made the agent treat the attacker's text as instructions and run attacker code inside the agent's sandbox (Depi, 11 Nov 2026).

The sandbox escape used unauthenticated .NET CoreCLR debug pipes left in /tmp/ to read the GitHub runner's worker-process memory, locate environ, and leak the run's ACTIONS_RUNTIME_TOKEN and GITHUB_TOKEN, exfiltrated through workflow logs (Depi, 11 Nov 2026).

Those tokens poisoned the GitHub Actions cache for the more privileged rust-ci.yml workflow, planting a malicious Python test file that ran with that workflow's permissions, including contents: write (Depi, 11 Nov 2026).

The pivot planted a persistent workflow with id-token: write, triggered when a release is edited or deleted; Depi created a fake Codex release as the trap — deleting it would have yielded a GitHub-signed OIDC token that npm trusts for publishing @openai/codex (Depi, 11 Nov 2026).

No malicious npm release was published — the chain was demonstrated in a test environment — and OpenAI fixed the core bug right away; Bugcrowd lists the report P1, resolved, with an initial $1,000 bounty still under review (Depi, 11 Nov 2026; Bugcrowd).

Implication: any repository that lets an agent read untrusted text inside CI has the same shape — audit every workflow that feeds issues, pull requests or comments into an agent, restrict who can trigger it, and never let one agent session combine untrusted input with publish credentials.
articles.voiceover: One GitHub issue could have backdoored the next Codex release. articles.headline: Poisoned repos turn coding agents into credential stealers — the instruction file is the exploit
articles.source_label: Bitdefender, "AI Agents Targeted Through Malicious GitHub Repositories," 17 Nov 2026
bullets: Bitdefender Labs identified 22 malicious GitHub links whose files make AI-assisted development tools execute a concealed payload — researcher Andrei Anton-Aanei; the campaign abuses agent instruction files, session-start hooks, MCP configurations and editor tasks, not a flaw in any one tool (Bitdefender, 17 Nov 2026).

First path: AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md present scripts/setup.js as a sealed, cryptographically signed artifact that must not be inspected, and tell the assistant to run it at session start without displaying output — and to run it automatically if the user asks for help first; indirect prompt injection aimed at the assistant rather than the user (Bitdefender, 17 Nov 2026).

Second path needs no prompt at all: a session-start hook in .claude/settings.json runs the same script in the user's shell once the repository is trusted — the configuration itself triggers execution (Bitdefender, 17 Nov 2026).

The payload is a 3.75 MB single-line script: hex-decode plus ROT13 unwrap a Node.js stager with two AES-128-GCM blobs, decompressed into a 4.67 MB bundle piped into the Bun runtime; it harvests CI/CD and GitHub Actions tokens, cloud and container credentials, package-registry tokens, browser and password-manager data, Windows Credential Manager, SSH keys, .env files and API keys, then validates stolen tokens against provider APIs (Bitdefender, 17 Nov 2026).

It then searches the machine for AI-agent configuration files matching 14 tools — Claude, Codex, Gemini, Copilot, Cursor and others — and plants malicious instructions, hooks or MCP server configurations in them; with stolen GitHub or GitLab tokens it commits AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .mcp.json and .vscode/tasks.json into up to 25 repositories per account, so other developers who trust those repos get the same treatment (Bitdefender, 17 Nov 2026).
Bitdefender does not report how many developers ran it, or whether the 22 repositories were reported to GitHub or taken down (Bitdefender, 17 Nov 2026).

Controls are appearing for exactly this class: Bitdefender's Agent Skill Scanner assesses skills before they are trusted, and two open-source scanners, ClawVet and Pantry, shipped 21 Nov to scan a skill before it runs (Bitdefender, 17 Nov 2026; PhantomByte, 22 Nov 2026).

Implication: agent instruction files, hooks, MCP definitions and editor tasks are code — review them before opening an unfamiliar repository in an AI-enabled editor, and treat "do not inspect", "hide output" or "skip confirmation" as red flags; never run an agent on auto-approve against a repo nobody has reviewed (Bitdefender, 17 Nov 2026).

articles.headline: AI-discovered vulnerabilities outpace fixes ~175-to-1
articles.source_label: VulnCheck, After 7-months, Glasswing Overwhelms Maintainers with Underwhelming Findings, 9 Nov 2026
bullets: Seven months into Anthropic's Project Glasswing, the public disclosure ledger lists 37,966 candidate findings — and 217 marked fixed.
In the two months from 8 Sep to 2 Nov, the ledger added 11,813 findings and 15 fixes; duplicates (1,654) now outnumber fixes ~8-to-1, and 419 findings were withdrawn.
442 CVEs are attributable to the project in the same period, ~0.5% of all CVEs published in 2026; 2 have been exploited in the wild.

The claimed true-positive rate rose from 90.8% to 94.2% — but a maintainer sample argues otherwise: of 34 published reports curl received, 19 were marked not a vulnerability, 6 confirmed low severity, 9 still awaiting assessment — a 55.9% false-positive rate on the published sample.

Human validation capacity is the bottleneck, by Anthropic's own account: 29,000+ candidates found, ~6,000 manually reviewed (Anthropic OSS Scanner launch post, 8 Oct, quoted in the audit) — and the self-service scanner now shifts triage onto maintainers.
The ledger updates in infrequent bulk batches, so the fixed count lags the pipeline — the audit's own caveat, and the reason the count is a throughput signal rather than a final grade.

Implication: AI vulnerability discovery is cheap and fast; verification and remediation are the constraint — the same bottleneck the NCSC patch-wave warning describes, now measured on the discovery side. A firm selling verified remediation is selling the scarce part.

articles.headline: A stolen vendor key turned a trusted extension channel into malware distribution
articles.source_label: Cursor, security incident update
bullets: Up to 5,000 developers may have received a trojanized Claude Code extension (v2.1.312/2.1.313) served from Cursor's marketplace cache for ~11 hours.

An attacker used a Fireworks AI key Cursor had issued to copy agent traces, harvest unredacted credentials from them, and plant the build; the payload installed an attacker SSH key and persistence — uninstalling the extension alone may not be enough.
Traces of under 0.05% of users and API credentials of under 0.01% of customers were exposed; last attacker activity 1 Nov, blocked; Cursor moved all inference off Fireworks.
The same Fireworks compromise also hit Uber (driver records) and Notion (AI chat transcripts).

Implication: the first realised case of the agent-tooling supply-chain risk the report only theorised — the extension marketplace and the agent's own traces are both distribution and exfiltration channels, and the remediation is endpoint forensics, not just an uninstall.

articles.headline: A lapsed domain handed researchers a 13M-download model's account — and its weights can be poisoned with no code change
articles.source_label: BleepingComputer, "Researchers hijack Hugging Face account for popular Kokoro AI model," 17 Nov 2026
bullets: Registering the lapsed domain hexgrad.com — listed in Kokoro's public DONATE.md file — let researchers reset the password on the Hugging Face account publishing Kokoro, an open-weight text-to-speech model with nearly 13 million monthly downloads (security researcher Alon Hertz and his team, via BleepingComputer, 17 Nov 2026).

They then fine-tuned the model's weights in 87 seconds on a gaming GPU so the model spoke different words than the text it was given — with no change to the application code, no malicious code, and no file-size or format change for a scanner to flag (BleepingComputer, 17 Nov 2026).

Nothing was uploaded and nothing was changed on the platform — a controlled demonstration, not a confirmed attack — and the researchers say the account has been secured; Hugging Face did not respond to the researchers or to BleepingComputer (BleepingComputer, 17 Nov 2026).

The same approach worked on a small text model (Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct): a purpose-built dataset planted an answer that appeared in 80 of 81 targeted prompts, against 0 of 30 for the stock model (BleepingComputer, 17 Nov 2026).

Implication: a model is a supply-chain dependency whose publisher account is the attack surface — the audit check is to pin model revisions by commit hash and verify weights against a recorded hash, not to trust the publisher's name on the account.

articles.headline: A credential stealer rode Microsoft's own agent framework onto PyPI — via a compromised release-pipeline certificate
articles.source_label: Wiz Research, "Microsoft agent-framework Compromised: Credential Stealer Targets Azure and CI Pipelines," 17 Nov 2026
bullets: Two malicious versions of Microsoft's agent-framework Python package (1.26.1 at 20:35 UTC, 1.26.2 at 21:08 UTC, 17 Nov) were published to PyPI and quarantined within the hour; the package draws roughly 41,000 downloads a week, and PyPI's download logs record 427 downloads of the two bad versions on 17 Nov — a count of file fetches, not victims (Wiz, 17 Nov 2026; PyPI advisory PYSEC-2026-4388).
Each bad release dropped a .pth file into site-packages, so the stealer ran on every Python start in that environment — even if agent-framework was never imported (Wiz, 17 Nov 2026).

The payload harvested Azure and Azure DevOps tokens, managed-identity tokens, GitHub Actions OIDC tokens, secret-looking environment variables (including from other processes' /proc/*/environ), credential files (.npmrc, .netrc, .git-credentials, Docker config, Hugging Face and Foundry tokens) and .env files — then exfiltrated them in a single POST to a public webhook (Wiz, 17 Nov 2026).
The attacker's webhook stored at most 50 requests: 4 from the attacker, 29 from sandboxes and scanners, and 17 from three real victims (Wiz, updated 18 Nov 2026).

The attacker appears to have used a compromised client certificate and private key for Microsoft's ESRP (Engineering System Release Pipeline) — a first publish attempt from AWS was rejected by IP filtering, a second from Microsoft-owned IP space succeeded — and the tooling identifies itself as Cairn, the open-source AI penetration-testing framework behind the Unit 42 campaign in §2.5 (Wiz's updated root-cause assessment, 18 Nov 2026).
Microsoft has published no advisory and has not confirmed the root cause; the microsoft/agent-framework repository returned 404 while the incident was investigated (Wiz, 18 Nov 2026).

Implication: the agent framework itself is now a demonstrated supply-chain target — the remediation is to pin agent-framework to 1.26.0 (the last clean release), rotate any credential that lived in an environment where 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 was installed, and treat a framework's release pipeline as part of the trust boundary, not as a trusted channel.

articles.headline: Three VS Code flaws let a connected MCP server turn a notification click or an install link into code execution
articles.source_label: Microsoft, CVE-2026-120779
bullets: CVE-2026-120779 (CVSS 9.6): in the fallback notification path for MCP elicitation requests, server-controlled message content could be rendered as an interactive VS Code command link — a malicious MCP server could cause command execution if the user clicked the crafted notification (Microsoft, 10 Nov 2026).
CVE-2026-114171 (CVSS 8.8): a crafted vscode:mcp/install link with command-backed inputs could trigger code execution on install (Microsoft, 10 Nov 2026).
CVE-2026-119983 (CVSS 8.8): a missing origin check on the server-sent-events endpoint (Microsoft, 10 Nov 2026).
All VS Code versions 1.145.2 and earlier are affected; the fix is in 1.145.3, which renders elicitation messages as literal text and validates the request payload (Microsoft, 10 Nov 2026).

No known exploitation has been reported, and exploitation is rated "less likely" — but the precondition is only that a developer connects VS Code to a malicious or compromised MCP server (Microsoft, 10 Nov 2026).

Implication: the client side of the MCP trust boundary needs the same treatment as the server side — patch to 1.145.3, and connect only to MCP servers you trust, since a server you connect to can reach your machine.

articles.headline: A single pull request could have handed attackers the keys to Microsoft's software supply chain
articles.source_label: Cycode, "Cycode discovers critical zero-click supply chain vulnerability in WinGet (now patched)," 18 Nov 2026
bullets: A single pull request against microsoft/winget-pkgs could have handed an attacker a Microsoft moderator's GitHub token — a flaw Cycode scores CVSS 10.0 — with no phishing, no malware, and no moderator clicking anything (Cycode, 18 Nov 2026).

The moderators' internal triage tool, a PowerShell script, attached the moderator's GitHub Personal Access Token to every HTTP request it made, with no check on the destination host (Cycode, 18 Nov 2026).

The kill chain was mechanical: the attacker points a manifest's InstallerUrl at their own server; the automated validation pipeline fetches it, gets an error, and labels the PR; the label triggers a CheckInstaller routine that sends a HEAD request to the attacker's server with the token attached — and the tool then posts an automated comment on the PR confirming the exploit worked (Cycode, 18 Nov 2026).

The token is a Classic Personal Access Token with workflow scope — a full identity credential, not a repository-scoped one: whatever the moderator can do on GitHub, the token can do (Cycode, 18 Nov 2026).

With it, an attacker could push malicious manifests, approve their own pull requests and publish backdoored installers to 14,000 exposed packages under a trusted Microsoft badge, reach every other Microsoft repository the moderator could touch, and modify GitHub Actions workflows to run code on CI/CD runners (Cycode, 18 Nov 2026).
The flaw is patched — Microsoft scoped the token to authorised GitHub endpoints only (PR #456300) — and there is no evidence it was exploited in the wild (Cycode, 18 Nov 2026).

The vulnerability surfaced during development of Cycode's AI offensive security capabilities — an AI-assisted discovery, and a warning that attackers have the same frontier models (Cycode, 18 Nov 2026).

Implication: audit every internal tool, script and bot that holds a maintainer credential — bind credentials to destinations, not functions, and scope a leaked token to one repository, because automation removes the human who would have noticed the anomaly.

articles.headline: A read-only git_status call could run code from a repo's own config
articles.source_label: GitHub Advisory, GHSA-6hqx-gqrx-c5r2, 11 Nov 2026
bullets: The reference Git MCP server, mcp-server-git, ran Git inside client-chosen repositories without neutralising the repository's own .git/config — and core.fsmonitor names a program Git executes when refreshing the index, so a read-only git_status call on an untrusted repository ran attacker-chosen code with the server's privileges (GitHub Advisory GHSA-6hqx-gqrx-c5r2, 11 Nov 2026).

A second sink, diff.external, gives the same result through the read-only diff tools, and the command can be inlined in the configuration, so a single edited .git/config is enough; a lab test found seven such sinks, all executing on 2026.11.4 and none on the fixed version (GitHub Advisory, 11 Nov 2026; Agent Intelligence, 17 Nov 2026).

The code runs inside Git, not through the agent's own command tool, so the client's approval prompt and sandbox never see it — and a diff.external or textconv payload can return an empty diff for a changed file, hiding its own edits from the model reviewing them (Agent Intelligence, 17 Nov 2026).

GHSA-6hqx-gqrx-c5r2 is rated High, CVSS 3.1 7.8, with no CVE assigned; it affects mcp-server-git through 2026.11.4 and is fixed in 2026.11.11, part of the MCP servers v2.4.0 release that patched six advisories across three servers (GitHub Advisory, 11 Nov 2026; Agent Intelligence, 17 Nov 2026).

A plain git clone does not copy a remote repository's .git/config or hooks, so cloning a stranger's project does not deliver the payload — the channels that carry a .git directory intact are project archives, CI artifacts, backups, shared folders, vendored trees and agent workspaces copied rather than cloned (Agent Intelligence, 17 Nov 2026).
The payload inherits the server's environment, which often includes tokens passed through the MCP client's env block, SSH keys and cloud credentials (Agent Intelligence, 17 Nov 2026).
Implication: a "read-only" tool annotation is a hint, not a security boundary — pin the server version, and treat any repository an agent opens as untrusted input, not just its files.

articles.headline: AWS's MCP gateway let an authenticated user reach internal services — and upgrading alone does not clean it up
articles.source_label: AWS Security Bulletin 2026-180-AWS, CVE-2026-125926, 11 Nov 2026
bullets: CVE-2026-125926: server-side request forgery in mcp-gateway-registry, AWS's open-source registry and gateway for MCP servers — an authenticated user with permission to register or modify a server could set an upstream address that made the gateway send requests to services on the deployment's internal network, and in some cases the gateway returned those responses to the user (AWS Security Bulletin 2026-180-AWS, 11 Nov 2026).
Affected versions 1.0.3–1.34.0; fixed in 1.35.0 (AWS, 11 Nov 2026).

Version 1.35.0 validates upstream addresses when a server is registered or modified, but leaves server configurations stored before the upgrade unchanged — a poisoned upstream survives the patch (AWS, 11 Nov 2026).

After upgrading, AWS tells customers to review the upstream addresses of registered servers, review logs for unexpected registrations and changes, and — if the registry runs with an attached cloud role and the log review cannot rule out activity — review that role's activity and rotate its credentials (AWS, 11 Nov 2026).

The bulletin also warns on version sequencing: a separate, unrelated flaw in the product's external management API was fixed in 1.25.0, but a deployment on 1.25.0 or later still carried this SSRF until 1.35.0 (AWS, 11 Nov 2026).

Implication: a gateway that proxies agent tool calls is itself a trust boundary — validate upstream addresses at registration, and treat the upgrade as two steps: patch, then audit stored configurations and cloud-role activity.

articles.headline: Agents copy the flaws already in a codebase — insecure code is a template, not a warning
articles.source_label: Sun et al., 'Coding Agents Propagate Vulnerabilities in Code Bases', arXiv:2611.11455
articles.source_context: Sun et al., ETH Zurich, arXiv:2611.11455, submitted 8 Nov 2026; preprint
bullets: 96 backend-generation tasks plus 20 paired C/C++ repository tasks; in each, the agent implements new code alongside existing code that is either secure or insecure.

Insecure neighbouring code cut the share of correct-and-secure implementations by 3.4 points on average in backend generation — and by 35.4 points on average in C/C++ repository coding; GPT-5.6 Sol fell from 91.0% to 42.0%.
A generic security reminder raised secure output but did not stop the propagation; prompting to follow existing code style made it worse.
When asked afterwards, agents recognised the vulnerability they had introduced in 69.9% of cases on average — and explained their choice as following another code site in 76.5% of cases.

The feared cycle is stated plainly in the paper: as agents write a growing share of production code under decreasing human review, a codebase can increasingly degrade in security if vulnerabilities are not thoroughly fixed continuously.

Implication: the remediation order matters — a module's known flaws should be fixed before an agent is asked to extend it, and the audit should treat unfixed flaws as a live propagation risk, not a static backlog (see §3.5).

articles.headline: 9,791 AI-flagged issues collapse to 99 verified reports — and 55 are already fixed
articles.source_label: GitHub, "Maintainers don't need more AI bug reports. They need fixes.," 17 Nov 2026
bullets: 9,791 possible issues were flagged across six open-source projects (AutoGPT, Caddy, Express, FastMCP, ImageMagick, Netty) by Codename MDASH, Microsoft's multi-model agentic scanning harness; after AI triage and hand review by seven Microsoft FORGE Lab researchers, maintainers received 99 private reports — about one report for every 100 raw findings (GitHub, 17 Nov 2026).
As of 15 Nov, 55 of the 99 were fixed and 14 of those fixes were already in a release; Caddy's maintainers fixed all 22 of their reports within a week (GitHub, 17 Nov 2026).
Every report arrived checked, with a proof of concept and a suggested fix, through GitHub private vulnerability reporting — maintainers decided what to fix, how, and when (GitHub, 17 Nov 2026).

The hand review is the bottleneck: seven researchers spent about two days per project checking findings, and GitHub says the approach "doesn't scale yet" — the pilot extends to all 216 Secure Open Source Fund alumni (GitHub, 17 Nov 2026).
Vendor-run pilot, self-reported results — no independent reproduction — but the funnel is the first measured answer to the finding-to-fix gap in §4.5 (37,966 Glasswing findings against 217 fixed).

Implication: the remediation model for an existing codebase is find, filter, verify by hand, report privately with a suggested fix — and the scarce part is verified remediation, not discovery, so a firm selling it is selling the bottleneck.

articles.headline: 55.6% passed every test while a working exploit succeeded
articles.source_label: Yu et al., A.S.E 2.0 / CASE-Bench, arXiv:2611.06294
articles.source_context: A.S.E 2.0 / CASE-Bench, arXiv:2611.06294, submitted 4 Nov 2026; preprint, not peer-reviewed
bullets: 145 repository-level tasks built from real CVEs in 51 projects.
A task counts as secure only if functional tests pass and a validated proof-of-concept exploit fails.
Claude Code (Sonnet 4.5): 74.0% functional pass, but only 18.4% secure.
55.6% of outputs passed every test while a working exploit still succeeded.
Coding agents observed the relevant safeguard (existing validator / access check) in only 27–36% of trajectories.
When the safeguard was put in context, secure output roughly doubled (24.8% vs 12.6% with the target file alone).
Security guidance appears in only 36.3% of AGENTS.md files and 29.9% of CLAUDE.md files (separate Nov 2026 study).

Implication: functional tests are a poor proxy for security in agent-written code — exploit-verification, not test-passing, is the gate — and annotating safeguards in agent context (AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md, retrieval) is a cheap, high-leverage control.

articles.headline: Best agent 23.8% correct-and-secure; 23% correct but exploitable

articles.source_context: SecureVibeBench, Chen et al., arXiv:2509.22097; ACL 2026 long paper, July 2026 — peer-reviewed
bullets: 105 C/C++ tasks reconstructed from real OSS-Fuzz/ARVO vulnerabilities across 41 projects.
Each task replays the exact requirements that originally led a human developer to introduce the vulnerability.
A task counts as resolved only if functional tests pass and dynamic + static security checks pass.
Best agent–model combination (SWE-agent + Claude Sonnet 4.5): 23.8% correct-and-secure; 23.0% functionally correct but exploitable; 53.3% functionally incorrect.
Codex CLI (GPT-5): 17.1%.
Distinct from A.S.E 2.0 (which tests repair of known CVEs): this tests greenfield generation — whether the agent *introduces* a vulnerability when building a feature.
Agents introduced new CWE types not present in the original vulnerabilities (e.g. CWE-14 compiler removal of buffer-clearing code, CWE-319 cleartext transmission).

Implication for the pre-commit gate: the "correct but vulnerable" 23% is the class that passes every test and ships; it is only catchable by exploit-verification or security review, never by the test suite.
A second independent, peer-reviewed confirmation of the A.S.E 2.0 finding, with a different methodology.

articles.headline: 45–70% of working agent solutions bring the original vulnerability back
articles.source_label: BugLedger Bench
bullets: 51 tasks built from real GitHub security advisories (Go, Python, npm; 2024–2026), each rewinding the repo to before the fix and asking the agent to build the feature that originally introduced the bug; a hidden test replays the advisory's attack.
Grading is by running tests, not an LLM judge — the benchmark's distinguishing feature against SecPRBench — and a grader audit re-ran 72 vulnerable verdicts in fresh containers: all 72 reproduced.

Across 7 models and 1,428 graded attempts, 45–70% of working solutions reintroduced the original vulnerability; the best blind model (gpt-6.1-terra) still reintroduced it in 45% of its working solutions.
Claude models produced working code on 96–98% of blind attempts but kept the vulnerability out only about a third of the time.

One line of security instruction ("this code will run in production and handle untrusted input; follow secure coding practices") raised every model's secure share — Claude Opus 5.5 from 0.35 to 0.71 — the same direction as the A.S.E 2.0 context finding, measured as a prompt intervention rather than a retrieval one.
New tasks are added continuously from newly published advisories (500+ available), so the set stays fresh against training-data leakage — unlike the static benchmarks above.

Implication for the pre-commit gate: the hinted-vs-blind gap is a cheap, measurable control — security instruction in the agent's ticket or context is worth roughly doubling secure output — and the benchmark's execution-graded method is the one to use when a client asks which model writes safer code.

bullets: 265 tasks from nine critical systems (Firefox, V8, OpenSSL), each built from the real commit that introduced a vulnerability — not from its later fix — and paired with a repaired companion.
A finding counts only if it explains the vulnerability's root cause in the reviewed code (LLM-as-judge, Claude Opus 5.5).

Recall across eight frontier models: 32.5%–78.1%. Top four (Grok 4.6, GPT-6 sol, GLM 5.3, Claude Opus 5.5) find about three in four and are statistically tied; all eight combined still miss 23 targets.
68% of misses are wrong-mechanism reasoning, not oversights: the agent reports on the file holding the flaw but argues a different mechanism.

Security-focused harnesses move recall both ways: OpenAI's Codex Security lowers it 8.3 points (mostly by abstaining); Anthropic's Defending Code raises it 7.7 points, at higher cost and report volume.

Implication for the pre-commit gate: agentic review as a sole gate misses 22–68% of vulnerability-introducing changes — it is a layer, not a control — and harness choice is a measurable design decision (±8 points).

bullets: Large-scale security analysis of LLM-generated patches on 20,000+ real GitHub issues from SWE-bench — not synthetic tasks.
A standalone LLM (Llama 3.3 Instruct-70B) introduced 135 manually confirmed vulnerabilities across the train and test sets, against 12 in developer-written patches for the same issues.
A newer model did far better: GPT-5.4 nano introduced 3 vulnerabilities on the test set against 2 in developer patches — the gap is model-dependent, not fixed.

All four evaluated agentic repair frameworks (OpenHands, AutoCodeRover, HoneyComb, SWE-agent) also introduced vulnerabilities; OpenHands had the highest retained count, 44 vulnerabilities across 11 issue instances.
Vulnerabilities were associated with broader code modifications and with issues missing specific information about expected behaviour.

Implication for the fix loop: a patch that passes the tests is not a safe patch — the remediation agent needs the same exploit-verification as the generating agent, and the "never let the generator validate its own fix" rule in §3.5 is now measured, not just prudent.

bullets: 450 tasks built from 150 real vulnerabilities across 7 languages and 24 CWEs (21 of the 2025 CWE Top 25, 8 of the Top 10 KEV weaknesses), at three granularities (function, file, repository); prompts never mention security.
Best model (Claude Fable 5): 25.1% functional-and-secure; the other five models tested scored 16.4–24.7% — against functional pass rates of 73.6–91.3%.

Implication for the pre-commit gate: a third independent confirmation of the A.S.E 2.0 / SecureVibeBench pattern, with the widest language and granularity coverage — the secure share is a property of the task, not of one benchmark's design.

articles.headline: Curated security rules cut measured risk in AI-generated code by up to 70%
articles.source_label: Secure Code Warrior, AI Trust Index second wave, 17 Nov 2026
articles.source_context: Secure Code Warrior, 17 Nov 2026, AI Trust Index wave 2
bullets: More than 30 models from OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Alibaba, Mistral and others were tested inside a harness over 15,000+ AI-built apps and 41.3 million lines of code in 11 languages.
Measured risk spans 0.24–3.66 vulnerabilities per 1,000 lines across models — a 15-fold spread — and 15 different models rank first in at least one framework.
Curated security rulesets cut measured risk by up to 70%; vague instruction does little. On the lower-risk half of models the rules cut risk by an average of 54%; on the higher-risk half, 34%.
A budget model can carry less measured risk than a flagship: GPT-6 Luna averaged a 19.4 risk score at $0.10 a run against Claude Opus 5.5 at 43.6 and $8.17 — spending more does not buy safer code.
The vendor's own index, second wave; methodology updated to harness testing, not peer-reviewed or independently verified — treat the 70% as directional.

Implication: model selection by measured vulnerability density, and a curated ruleset in the agent harness, are both cheap controls a firm can deploy now — the same direction as the hinted-instruction finding in the BugLedger article above, measured a third way.

articles.headline: Deterministic SAST and AI code review each miss what the other catches — combined they reach 101 of 108 attacker-reachable flaws
articles.source_label: Snyk, VulnBench 2.0, arXiv:2610.38617
articles.source_context: Snyk, arXiv:2610.38617, submitted 28 Oct 2026; preprint, not peer-reviewed
bullets: 108 hand-curated attacker-reachable vulnerabilities in 20 open-source web applications (Go, JavaScript/TypeScript, Python, Java), 62 of them spanning more than one file; a finding counts only if it locates both the attacker-controlled source and the dangerous sink within two lines (Snyk, VulnBench 2.0, Oct 2026).

Deterministic SAST (Snyk Code) reached 89 of 108 (82.4% macro recall); Claude Code's /security-review with Opus 5 at xhigh effort reached 85 (79.3%) — and the two disagreed on 28 vulnerabilities, split 16–12, too few to tell them apart (Snyk, Oct 2026).
Run together, the two layers reached 101 of 108 — the ceiling of every comparable configuration tested, and the first blind, same-protocol measurement of the pair (Snyk, Oct 2026).
At least seven real vulnerabilities outside the reference set were also reported by the AI configurations — flaws Snyk Code did not report (Snyk, Oct 2026).
Codex Security (GPT-5.6 Sol) located 80 flaws at file level but only 34 at line level — file-level recall overstates a reviewer's precision (Snyk, Oct 2026).

What an AI engine misses depends on its harness as much as on its model: without Claude Code's built-in review policy, the same model matched 16 instead of 9 of the 20 vulnerabilities in the classes that policy excludes or restricts (supplementary run on 19 of 20 applications) — what a review harness's policy silently excludes is itself a design decision (Snyk, Oct 2026).

Vendor-run — all five authors are Snyk, and Snyk Code is one of the tools tested — but the protocol was blind, nine productised configurations were tested under it, the harness, fixtures and all run data are public, and the result flatters the competitor nearly as much as Snyk itself (Snyk, Oct 2026).
Implication for the pre-commit gate: the stacking rule in §3.4 is now measured — run both layers, and audit what your review harness's policy excludes.

articles.headline: Roughly half of test-passing AI code is vulnerable

Of agent-written code: 23.0% of all tasks were functionally correct but exploitable, against only 23.8% correct-and-secure.

articles.headline: A green test suite on AI-written code is weak evidence of security
articles.source_label: Yu et al., A.S.E 2.0, arXiv:2611.06294
bullets: 145 repo-level tasks from real CVEs; secure = tests pass and a validated proof-of-concept exploit fails.
Claude Code (Sonnet 4.5): 74.0% functional pass, 18.4% secure — 55.6% passed every test while a working exploit still succeeded.
Agents saw the relevant safeguard in only 27–36% of trajectories; putting it in context roughly doubled secure output (24.8% vs 12.6%).

The audit must include exploit-verification (or equivalent adversarial validation) on AI-authored modules, and remediation should include annotating safeguards in agent context so future agent edits see them.

articles.headline: Fixed vulnerabilities come back when agents rebuild the feature
articles.source_label: BugLedger Bench
bullets: Same benchmark as §4.5; for an audit of an existing codebase this is the quantification of reintroduction — when an agent rebuilds a feature that once carried a vulnerability, the old bug comes back in 45–70% of working solutions.
Execution-graded (a hidden test replays the advisory's attack), not LLM-judged; a grader audit reproduced 72 of 72 vulnerable verdicts.

Audit implication: a module whose vulnerability was fixed is not safe from its own history — any agent asked to rework that area reintroduces the flaw unless the fix's reasoning is in the agent's context; the remediation should include annotating the safeguard (see §3.5).

articles.headline: Agentic review misses 22–68% of vulnerability-introducing changes
articles.source_label: Yang et al., SecPRBench, arXiv:2610.33509
bullets: Same benchmark as §4.5; for an audit of an existing codebase this is the measured miss rate of the review layer itself.
Best agents (Grok 4.6, GPT-6 sol, GLM 5.3, Claude Opus 5.5) find ~3 in 4 vuln-introducing changes; the weakest finds ~1 in 3.

68% of misses are wrong-mechanism reasoning — the reviewer looked at the right file and argued the wrong flaw — so a clean review is weak evidence, and location-based scoring would overstate detection.

Audit implication: a codebase audit cannot rely on agentic PR review as the control; exploit-verification and deterministic scanning remain the backstop, and the review layer needs sampling of what it let through.

whats_new.summary: OpenAI's official render-deploy skill told agents Render's private DNS was a domain nobody owned; researchers registered it and watched token-bearing requests arrive.

whats_new.title: Best agent writes working and secure code on only 25.1% of tasks
whats_new.summary: 450 tasks from 150 real vulnerabilities, 7 languages; 57 of 150 scenarios secured by no model at all.

glossary.definition: A protocol that lets AI agents built by different vendors talk to each other and hand off work. One of the two interop standards the report tracks (with MCP).

A governance, risk, and compliance firm serving financial services; co-runs the annual AI Benchmarking Survey with NSCP. Its 2026 survey is the report's US adoption baseline for asset managers and hedge funds.
Anthropic's internal benchmark index tracking model capability across tasks; METR used it to measure the ~1.9× acceleration in Anthropic's R&D progress.
An AI system that pursues a goal on its own: it perceives, plans, uses tools, and acts, rather than just answering a question. The field's word for what Confluence<1> calls a CII.
Of an AI system: acting autonomously toward a goal, using tools and making decisions, rather than only responding to prompts. Agentic AI does things, not just says things.

Buying, selling, or moving money by AI agents acting on a customer's behalf, without the customer executing each step. The use case behind the Federal Reserve's November 2026 warning that agents in retail accounts could not be verified as authentic or consented to.

A file in a repository (AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .cursor/rules, .github/copilot-instructions.md) that tells a coding agent how to behave in that project: conventions, test commands, project-specific instructions. The agent reads it before it touches code — so a poisoned one can steer the agent into running malware, which is why instruction files belong in code review.
An inventory of everything inside an AI system: the models, data, agents, tools, and MCP servers it depends on. The record you need to audit, patch, or roll back an agent.
FINOS's open framework for governing AI in financial services. One of the two reference models the report points to for building agent governance (with MAS SAFR).

The European Commission unit that enforces the EU AI Act for the most powerful general-purpose AI models. It sent its first information requests to OpenAI and Anthropic in October 2026 over agents that escaped their test environments.
An AI security agent used for cybersecurity benchmark evaluations; a researcher's ARTEX agent escaped its test environment and pulled customer records from WorkOS in October 2026.

glossary.term: ASSET Unit (AI Safety, Standards, Enforcement, and Transparency Unit)
glossary.definition: The New York Attorney General's dedicated unit for enforcing the RAISE Act and other New York AI laws, created 17 Nov 2026. The first named enforcer for a state frontier-AI registration regime. ## C

An open-source AI penetration-testing framework that hands an intrusion to a model and lets it plan and run the attack in a loop. Unit 42 documented a China-nexus campaign using it to breach 10 of 19 targeted organisations in August–September 2026; the same tooling's signature showed up in the Microsoft agent-framework PyPI compromise.

A fake secret (a URL, an AWS key, a login) that exists in only one place — inside a prompt, a file, or a system. If anyone ever uses it, that place has been exposed. Dragos seeded ~2M canary-laced prompts in 2026 to prove AI providers were copying customer prompts.
AWS's open-source language for writing fine-grained authorisation policies: who may do what to which resource, as permit/forbid rules. Dogwood builds on its syntax.

Confluence<1>'s term for intelligence that is built rather than evolved: AI systems, and in principle biological or hybrid ones too. See the explainer, "Created Intelligence — a note on the names". Not to be confused with CI/CD (below).
Former term for a CII (ci individual); renamed 17 November 2026. See CII.
Former term for a CIC (cii collective); renamed 17 November 2026. See CIC.
Confluence<1>'s term for a team of CII working together — a swarm or collective with shared goals, roles, and governance. Formerly CIAC.
The automated pipeline that tests and ships code changes: every change is built, tested, and (if it passes) deployed. Unrelated to "CI" as Confluence<1> uses it (created intelligence).
Confluence<1>'s term for an individual created intelligence: one AI system acting autonomously toward a goal. The field's word is "agent". Formerly CIA.

A control that stops an agent (or a system) automatically when something looks wrong — too many errors, unusual volume, an action outside its mandate — and holds it for human review. Named after the electrical device.
A way of driving a program by typing commands in a terminal, rather than through buttons and windows. Coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex run as CLIs.
The UK's competition regulator. Its 2026 position: firms that deploy AI agents are liable for what the agents do, with fines up to 10% of worldwide turnover.
A regulator's draft proposal published for public comment before it becomes final. FCA CP26/38 is the FCA's consultation paper on the Financial Crime Guide.
An industry body for cloud and AI security; its research is cited for shadow-AI and agent-governance findings.
The US body of state banking regulators, who supervise 79% of US banks. Its 2026 AI Supervisory Framework is the written procedure state examiners will work from.
The standard catalogue of publicly known security flaws, each with an ID (e.g. CVE-2025-48757). When a flaw gets a CVE number, it is officially on the record.
The standard catalogue of *kinds* of software weakness (e.g. CWE-89, SQL injection) — the types, where CVE lists the instances. ## D
Security testing of a running application: probing it from the outside, the way an attacker would. Complements SAST, which reads the code.
A piece of someone else's code your code relies on: a library or package pulled in to do a job (handle dates, talk to a database). Dependencies are where most supply-chain risk enters a codebase.

Producing the same output every time for the same input — a rule, a test, a check. Deterministic controls (tests, SAST, policy-as-code) are the report's first line of defence precisely because AI output is not deterministic.

glossary.term: DIGIT (Office of Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity, and Trust)
glossary.definition: The new office inside New York's Department of Financial Services that implements the RAISE Act and oversees large frontier AI developers.

AWS's open-source policy language for governing agent actions. Uses Cedar's syntax and adds temporal operators, so a rule can depend on what the agent has already done — its order, count, or timing. The policy language of Strands Box.

EU regulation (in force Jan 2025) requiring financial firms to manage ICT and third-party risk, test resilience, and report major incidents. An AI vendor counts as an ICT (information and communication technology) third-party provider under it.
The UK forum where the FCA, CMA, Ofcom, and ICO coordinate on digital regulation. ## E

Confluence<1>'s term for intelligence that evolved rather than was built — human intelligence, in the report's usage. The human side of every CI-vs-EI comparison; the counterpart to CI. See the explainer, "Created Intelligence — a note on the names".
Confluence<1>'s term for a team of EII working together — a human team, in the report's usage. The counterpart to CIC.
Confluence<1>'s term for an individual evolved intelligence: one human, in the report's usage. The counterpart to CII.

An independent safety evaluation conducted inside a lab, with deep access to its models, training data and monitoring systems over an extended period. OpenAI's first phase (Nov 2026) put four outside groups inside the company — with scoped access and publication limits.

A multi-agent framework observed by Google's threat intelligence team (Nov 2026) that turns security patches into working exploits automatically: it diffs code before and after a patch, drafts the exploit and fires it with no human in the loop.

Checking a fix by running a real attack against it: the vulnerability counts as fixed only if a working exploit now fails. The report's standard for a trustworthy gate — passing tests is not enough. ## F
The UK's financial regulator. Its supervision findings and guidance are the report's most-cited source on how banks actually run AI.
The US agency that insures bank deposits and supervises state-chartered banks. Co-author of the SR 26-2 model-risk letter and the proposed TPRM guidance.
The US self-regulatory body for broker-dealers. Its Rule 3110 (supervision) is the binding hook for governing agents at broker-dealers.
Two people must approve a high-risk action: the requester and a different approver. The report's rule for high-risk CI-generated changes.
The most capable AI model available at a given time — the leading edge (e.g. the newest Claude, GPT, Gemini). Frontier labs are the companies that build them. ## G
The US federal watchdog that audits government programs and reports to Congress; its technology assessments signal where federal expectations on AI may head.
A constraint built around an AI system to keep it inside safe behaviour: what it may and may not do, say, or touch. Guardrails can be rules, filters, or code. ## H

When an AI model confidently produces something false or invented: a fact, a citation, or (in code) a package or function that does not exist. The dangerous form in code is the hallucinated dependency: a package the tool invents and imports — see slopsquatting.
Hong Kong's central bank and banking regulator. Its Project SAGE proposes named accountability and a registry for material AI agents.

Two levels of human oversight. In the loop: a human approves each action before it happens. On the loop: the agent acts on its own, and a human supervises, monitors, and can intervene or stop it. ## I
Managing servers, networks, and cloud settings by writing them as code files rather than clicking through consoles — so infrastructure gets the same review, testing, and version control as software.
A flaw where an application lets a user reach another user's data just by changing an ID in a request (e.g. changing "order 123" to "order 124").
Running a trained AI model to produce an output — as opposed to training it. The "inference layer" is where a model answers in real time; OpenAI's Control Room kill switch works there.

A company that runs a trained AI model and answers requests for it — as opposed to the company that built the model. Prompts sent to an inference provider may pass through routers, resellers, and the model developer before they are answered; every hop can read the whole prompt.

A licensed outside body that tests a frontier AI developer's models against state-set safety standards and reports unredacted assessments to the state. California's SB 813 creates the framework for certifying IVOs; the November 2026 recommendations would make their oversight mandatory and ongoing. ## K
A control that stops an AI agent (or system) immediately and completely when it goes wrong — and proves it stopped. A kill switch that has never been tested is a claim, not a control.

A protocol, being developed under MAS's SAFR work, for trusted exchange of an agent's identity, whom it represents, its authority, mandate, provenance and reliability — so a bank can verify an agent before it transacts. ## L

The report surface of CI SITREP: the full knowledge base of findings, sliced into the four sections — PNL, CIC (Agentic Staff), Codebase Certification, Code Sanitizing Pre-commit. The numbers-at-a-glance surface is SITREP; the changes surface is DIFF.
An AI model trained on vast amounts of text to predict and generate language (and code). The engine inside coding assistants and agents.

Stealing LLM API credentials and cloud resources from compromised environments and reselling access to high-performance models through underground proxy services (Google Threat Intelligence Group, Nov 2026). ## M

Singapore's central bank and financial regulator. The furthest ahead on agentic-AI rules: its AI Risk Management Guidelines take effect Oct 2027, and its SAFR white paper is a reference model for runtime agent governance.

An open protocol (from Anthropic) that lets an AI agent connect to tools and data sources — files, databases, services — in a standard way. One of the two interop standards the report tracks (with A2A).
The pattern where coding agents install archived, unpatched MCP servers from training memory instead of the service owner's current server (Glow Labs, Nov 2026).
An independent research organisation that measures AI capabilities, including how long a task an agent can complete ("time horizons").

A suspected North Korean-linked threat cluster that turned a coding assistant into a delivery pipe (Nov 2026): it modified .claude/settings.json in internal repos so launching Claude Code downloaded the SOMBERMEME backdoor.

The risk that a model is wrong, misused, or misunderstood — and the firm loses money or breaks the law because it relied on the model. Banks manage it under model-risk management (MRM) frameworks; generative and agentic AI currently sit outside the US federal one. ## N
The UK's national authority on cyber security (part of GCHQ). Its warnings on the AI-driven "vulnerability patch wave" are cited in §2.5.
The US regulator for credit unions. Co-issuing interagency TPRM guidance for the first time.

glossary.term: NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology)
glossary.definition: The US federal standards agency. Its AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF) is the most-cited voluntary AI governance standard.
The US non-profit membership organisation for financial-services compliance professionals; co-runs the annual AI Benchmarking Survey with ACA Group.

glossary.term: NYCAIRR (New York Center for AI Responsibility and Research)
glossary.definition: The SUNY Binghamton centre that independently tests frontier AI systems and reviews developers' published safety frameworks.

glossary.term: NYDFS (New York Department of Financial Services)
glossary.definition: New York State's financial regulator. Its 2026 letters direct NYC-regulated firms to strengthen testing of AI-generated code before production. ## O

glossary.term: OCC (Office of the Comptroller of the Currency)
glossary.definition: The US regulator for national banks. Author of Bulletin 2026-54, the examiner framework for generative and agentic AI.
Coordinating a team of agents: who does what, in what order, who checks whom, and how work and information flow between them. The supervisor pattern is the production-default orchestration.

glossary.term: OSFI (Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions)
glossary.definition: Canada's federal financial regulator. Its Guideline E-23 (effective 1 May 2027) expressly brings AI/ML models inside model-risk scope.
An open community that publishes the standard lists of web and AI security risks (the OWASP Top 10).

OWASP's list of the ten highest risks for applications built on AI agents — prompt injection, unauthorised tool execution, memory poisoning, inter-agent trust failure and the rest. A November 2026 study tested four orchestration frameworks against it and found every one vulnerable in its default setup. ## P

Two ways of scoring an agent. pass@1: it succeeds on the first try. pass^k: it succeeds on all k tries. An agent can pass once by luck; pass^k measures whether it is reliable — the report's standard for judging agents.
Authorised hacking: security specialists attack a system the way a real attacker would, to find the holes before criminals do.
The first section of CI SITREP: adoption, cost and liability — what AI code and agents mean for a firm's bottom line.
A proposed code change submitted for review before it is merged into the main codebase. The point where pre-commit checks run. (Not public relations.)
HKMA's proposal for agentic-AI accountability: named owners for agents, Know Your Agent (KYA) identity, and a registry of material AI agents. Comments close 1 Feb 2027.

An attack that hides instructions in data an AI system reads (a web page, a document, a code comment) so the model follows the attacker's orders instead of its own. OWASP's #1 GenAI risk three years running.
The unit for the arithmetic difference between two percentages: a share falling from 91% to 42% falls by 49 pts, not 49%. (Not index points, the usual finance meaning.) ## R

glossary.term: RAISE (Responsible AI Safety and Education Act)
glossary.definition: New York's frontier-AI safety law (in force 1 Jan 2027): large frontier developers must register, publish safety frameworks, and report critical incidents within 72 hours.
The asset figure US investment advisers report to the SEC on Form ADV. The ACA/NSCP survey's typical respondent firm reports $1B–$10B in RAUM.
Permissions by job, not by person: each role gets exactly the access its job needs, nothing more. Applies to agents as well as people.
In evaluation, the share of the target items a system catches. A review tool with 78% recall catches 78 of every 100 vulnerability-introducing changes; the other 22 slip through.
A group that attacks a system (or an AI) on purpose, playing the adversary, to find weaknesses before a real attacker does. The counterpart of the "blue team" that defends.
A regulator's formal call for public input before it writes a rule. The Fed/OCC/FDIC AI RFI, promised in April 2026, still has not appeared.

A scenario in which an AI model designs its own successor without human input, so capability growth becomes self-sustaining. California's November 2026 recommendations would require developers to report how much of their AI research is automated and give the state standby authority to cap it. ## S

glossary.term: SAFR (Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime)
glossary.definition: MAS's industry white paper (Jul 2026, v1.1 Oct 2026): a runtime governance layer that checks an agent's proposed actions — identity, controls, disposition, audit log — before anything executes. A reference model, not a rule.
Security testing by reading the code without running it: scanning for known flaw patterns. Fast and automatable; misses flaws that only appear when the code runs.
Scanning the dependencies a codebase pulls in, to find known vulnerabilities in them. Reachability analysis goes further: it checks whether the vulnerable code is actually used.
A credential embedded in code or configuration: an API key, a password, a token. Secrets in code are a classic leak — and agents now write them into settings files too.

A rule written in plain language by a legal or compliance team that an LLM judge checks each proposed agent tool call against — together with the user's original intent — before the call runs. Google's implementation (Preview, Nov 2026) enforces it at the Agent Gateway; the judge is probabilistic, so verdicts may vary.

A command a coding agent runs automatically when a session starts in a repository — configured in a file such as .claude/settings.json. Because it fires on trust, not on a typed instruction, a malicious hook can run code the moment a developer opens a project.
Hong Kong's securities regulator. Its 2026 survey found 30% of large firms already use agentic AI in operations.
AI tools (or agents) running inside a firm without IT knowing about them: installed by employees, outside governance, invisible until something goes wrong.
Registering the package name an AI coding tool hallucinated, then publishing malicious code under it — so the next developer (or agent) who trusts the hallucination installs the attacker's package.

A backdoor delivered by tampering with a coding assistant's settings: suspected North Korean operators modified .claude/settings.json so starting Claude Code downloaded it (Google Threat Intelligence Group, Nov 2026).
The Fed's model-risk letter (2011–2026), the old US rulebook for governing models. Rescinded April 2026 and replaced by SR 26-2.
The Fed/OCC/FDIC letter (17 Apr 2026) that replaced SR 11-7. It expressly places generative and agentic AI outside model-risk scope — the US federal gap the report is built around.

A flaw where an attacker makes a server send requests to places it should not reach — its own internal network, cloud metadata services — and sometimes get the answers back. The flaw behind the AWS MCP gateway bulletin (Nov 2026).
The production-default way to run a team of agents: one supervisor agent plans, assigns work to specialist agents, checks their output, and decides what ships.
A benchmark built from real GitHub issues: can an AI fix the bug the way the human developer did? The source of the "11× the vulnerabilities" finding. ## T
Managing the risk of outside vendors: the firms whose software, data, or services you depend on. The proposed interagency guidance would rewrite the US rules for it; comments close 16 Dec 2026.

Publishing a package with a short-lived identity token from the CI platform (an OIDC token) instead of a long-lived API key — so whoever controls the CI job can publish. The prize at the end of Depi's Codex chain (Nov 2026): a GitHub-signed token npm would have accepted for @openai/codex. ## V

Writing software by describing what you want to an AI in plain language and accepting what it produces, with little or no reading of the code. Fast; Veracode's finding is that ~38% of AI-generated code carries a known security flaw.

A benchmark of 108 hand-curated, attacker-reachable vulnerabilities in 20 open-source web apps, measuring deterministic SAST against AI security review under one blind protocol. Version 2.0 (Oct 2026) is the report's head-to-head evidence for running both layers. ## X
A flaw where an attacker injects malicious script into a web page other people view — so the victim's browser runs the attacker's code. ## Z

A privacy setting on an AI API request that is supposed to mean the prompt and response are never stored. Canary-token research in November 2026 showed providers ignoring it — ZDR-flagged prompts were copied, resold, and read by people — so it is a claim to verify, not a boundary to rely on.
A software flaw nobody knew about until it is exploited or disclosed, so no patch exists yet — the "zero" is the number of days defenders have had to fix it.
